name: Stripe
summary: Stripe publishes its operating principles, such as Users first and Move with urgency and focus, and says most hiring processes include a recruiter screen, a technical or skills-based assessment and interviews with the team. Its engineering interviews are known for practical work rather than whiteboard puzzles; Stripe has described a 'Bug Squash' interview in which candidates fix a historical bug in an open-source project.
rounds: Onsite: practical coding (debugging, building against an API), system design, and behavioral interviews

questions.text: Tell me about a bug you tracked down that others couldn't.
covers: The symptom and why it was hard to pin down
Your method: reproducing it, narrowing it down, testing ideas one at a time
The cause, the fix, and what stopped it coming back

questions.text: How would you design an API that lets businesses refund a payment safely?
covers: Idempotency keys so a retried request doesn't refund twice
Checks: refund no more than was paid, partial refunds, refunds while a payment is pending
Clear errors, status updates by webhook, and a record for reconciliation

questions.text: Tell me about a time you did more for a user than your role asked.
covers: Who the user was and what they actually needed
What you did beyond your role, and why it was worth it
The result for the user

questions.text: Tell me about something you wrote, such as a design doc or post-mortem, that changed what your team did.
covers: The decision or problem the document addressed
How you structured it so busy readers got the point
What the team did differently because of it

questions.text: Tell me about a piece of work you're proud of for its craft, not only its result.
covers: What made it well made: the details users or teammates would notice
The extra effort it took and why you chose to spend it
How it held up over time

questions.text: Tell me about a time you changed course because someone else's idea was better than yours.
covers: Your idea and theirs, described fairly
What convinced you
How you supported their approach and credited them

questions.text: What is idempotency, and how would you make a payment request safe to retry?
covers: Idempotency in plain words: doing it twice has the same effect as once
A client-supplied key, stored with the result so a retry returns the same answer
Why it matters: timeouts and network failures leave the client unsure what happened

questions.text: How would you design a system that delivers webhooks to merchants reliably, even when their servers are down?
covers: A queue of events with retries and growing backoff
Signing payloads so merchants can verify them, and handling duplicates on their side
Visibility: delivery logs, alerts, and letting merchants replay missed events

questions.text: You're handed an unfamiliar codebase and a failing test. Talk me through how you'd find the cause.
covers: Reading the test and the error first, then reproducing it
Narrowing down: logs, a debugger, recent changes
Stating a hypothesis, checking it, and fixing the cause rather than the symptom

questions.text: How would you design a ledger that records money moving between accounts so the books balance?
covers: Double-entry records: every movement debits one account and credits another
Entries that are never edited, only corrected by new entries
Reconciliation with banks, and handling currencies and rounding

questions.text: What makes an API pleasant for developers to integrate? Give examples of good and bad design.
covers: Consistent naming, predictable resources and useful error messages
Versioning so changes don't break existing integrations
Docs, test modes and examples that get someone to a first success quickly

questions.text: How would you help a small online business reduce failed payments at checkout?
covers: Finding where and why payments fail: declines, errors, abandoned steps
Fixes such as local payment methods, retrying soft declines and a simpler form
Measuring conversion while watching fraud and refunds

questions.text: Why Stripe, and which of its products or users interest you most?
covers: A specific product or user group and the problem Stripe solves for them
A link to your own experience
What you'd want to build or improve

questions.text: Which of Stripe's operating principles fits how you like to work, and which would stretch you most?
covers: One principle, named accurately, with a short example
An honest stretch area and how you're working on it
Why Stripe's way of working suits you

tips: Practise practical tasks (reading code, fixing bugs, calling an API), not just puzzles.
Talk about correctness: idempotency and failure modes matter in payments.
Stripe says it shares written guides before interviews; read yours closely, as it explains the format and how to prepare.
Stripe has written that engineers can use their own laptop and development environment; know your editor, tests and debugger well.
Try Stripe's API documentation and test mode before the interview so building against an API feels familiar.

sources.title: Stripe Atlas: scaling engineering organisations (interview practices)
